lead: Blood hitting a closing valve makes a short, low thump. A stethoscope lets a doctor hear this directly; a phonocardiograph records it as a waveform, the PCG, beside the ECG. The ECG says when the heart electrically fired; the PCG says when the valves actually shut. Clinicians use heart sounds at every bedside examination and in foetal monitoring. Engineers use them to test microphones, filters and timing circuits. This chapter explains where S1 and S2 come from, how the stethoscope couples sound to the ear, and how the PCG signal chain times sounds against the ECG.
prereq: You need: ECG recording, bio-amplifiers and filter basics (see ECG recording system and vector cardiography, and Bio-amplifiers and data acquisition systems).

sections.h3: What makes the sounds, and when

blocks.text: A heart sound is a short vibration from the heart and great vessels. S1 and S2 come from a valve closing; S3 and S4 come from blood entering the ventricle. The leaflet stops, the blood column behind it is checked, and a pressure wave runs through the chest wall. Valve opening is normally quiet. Systole is the phase when the ventricles contract; diastole is when they relax and fill.

S1 is the first sound. It comes from closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole. Its two parts are M1 and T1. S2 comes from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole; its parts are A2 and P2. S3 is a low sound in early diastole, when blood rushes into the ventricle. S4 is a low sound in late diastole, when the atrium contracts. S3 is common in children and young adults and is often harmless. S4 can be normal in children and athletes, but in an older adult it usually means a stiff ventricle and suggests disease.

Most of the energy of S1 and S2 lies below about 200 Hz, and S3 and S4 sit at the very low end, below about 50 Hz. Murmurs come from turbulent flow and spread higher, to several hundred hertz, but they vary: aortic stenosis and regurgitation are relatively high-pitched, while mitral stenosis is a low-pitched rumble that needs the bell. That is why a stethoscope needs two chest pieces, and why a phonocardiograph offers more than one filter band.

A stethoscope has a chest piece, tubing and earpieces. It does not amplify sound in the electronic sense; it couples the small pressure changes at the chest wall to the ear canal with as little loss as possible. The ear then does the hearing.

The bell is an open cup. It senses low-frequency pressure changes and is used for S3, S4 and low murmurs such as mitral stenosis. Press it lightly. Pressing hard stretches the skin under it and turns the skin into a diaphragm, so low sounds fade. The diaphragm is a stretched membrane. It responds to higher-frequency movement and is used for S1, S2 and higher murmurs such as aortic regurgitation. Press it firmly.

Tubing matters. A long, narrow or thin-walled tube attenuates high frequencies and adds resonances. Keep the tube short, wide and thick-walled, and seal the earpieces in the ear. A noisy room raises the noise floor, so quiet low sounds are lost first. A stethoscope is a coupling device, not a gain device.

sections.h3: Phonocardiograph: recording the sound with time reference

blocks.text: A phonocardiograph records the heart sound as a waveform. The chain is: chest piece, microphone, preamplifier, band-pass filter, amplifier, recorder or display. An air-coupled microphone has a small air chamber closed by a membrane; chest vibration moves the membrane and changes the air pressure on a capacitive or electret element. A contact microphone, often piezoelectric, sits directly on the chest. The preamplifier needs high input impedance so it does not load the microphone.

The band-pass filter keeps the heart-sound band and rejects baseline wander below about 25 Hz and high-frequency noise above its upper cutoff. The worked example uses 25 Hz to 400 Hz. A narrow upper cutoff makes a clean trace but can hide a high-frequency murmur. The amplifier raises the signal to a level the recorder can handle.

A simultaneous ECG channel is the time reference. The R wave marks electrical activation. S1 and S2 follow the R wave by short, repeatable delays that are measured on each trace; the S2 delay in particular lengthens as the heart rate falls. On the trace, a systolic murmur lies between S1 and S2; a diastolic murmur lies between S2 and the next S1. A2 and P2 can separate on inspiration, giving a split S2. Heart rate is found from the RR interval: heart rate in beats per minute = 60 / RR, with RR in seconds. Foetal phonocardiography uses the same idea to separate the baby's sounds from the mother's; see Chapter 2.4.

figure.caption: The ECG gives the time reference: S1 starts 0.05 s and S2 0.35 s after the R wave, so systole lasts 0.30 s and diastole 0.50 s of the 0.80 s cycle.

spec.aria: An ECG trace above a phonocardiogram; S1 at 0.05 s and S2 at 0.35 s after the R wave, systole 0.30 s, diastole 0.50 s, RR 0.80 s and heart rate 75 beats per minute.

examples.question: A phonocardiogram is recorded with a 25-400 Hz filter together with lead II ECG. S1 begins 0.05 s after the R wave, S2 begins 0.35 s after the same R wave, and the next R wave comes 0.80 s later. (a) Find the systolic interval. (b) Find the heart rate and the diastolic interval. (c) Would a 600 Hz murmur appear on this trace?
steps: (a) The systolic interval is the time from S1 onset to S2 onset: 0.35 s − 0.05 s = 0.30 s.
(b) The RR interval is 0.80 s. Heart rate = 60 / RR = 60 / 0.80 = 75 beats per minute.
Diastolic interval = RR − systolic interval = 0.80 s − 0.30 s = 0.50 s.
(c) The filter upper cutoff is 400 Hz. A 600 Hz component lies above this cutoff and is heavily attenuated, so it does not show on the trace.
examples.answer: The systolic interval is 0.30 s, the heart rate is 75 beats per minute, the diastolic interval is 0.50 s, and the 600 Hz murmur is largely removed by the 400 Hz upper cutoff.
examples.check:
s1 = 0.05
s2 = 0.35
rr = 0.80
systolic = s2 - s1
hr = 60 / rr
diastolic = rr - systolic
print(systolic)
print(hr)
print(diastolic)

traps: Saying S2 is caused by valve opening. S1 and S2 both come from valve closure; S2 is the aortic and pulmonary valves shutting at the end of systole.
Pressing the bell hard and still expecting low sounds. Heavy pressure turns the skin into a diaphragm and removes S3 and S4.
Putting a systolic murmur after S2. Systole lies between S1 and S2; diastole lies between S2 and the next S1.
Using a PCG upper cutoff that is too low. A clean-looking trace can hide a high-frequency murmur above the cutoff.
Using RR in milliseconds in heart rate = 60/RR. Either convert RR to seconds, or use 60000/RR with RR in milliseconds.

quiz.q: Which valves close to produce S1, and which close to produce S2?
quiz.a: S1 comes from closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole. S2 comes from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole.

quiz.q: Why is the bell used for S3 and S4, while the diaphragm is used for S1 and S2?
quiz.a: The bell responds to low-frequency pressure changes, and S3 and S4 are low-frequency sounds. The diaphragm responds to higher-frequency movement, and S1 and S2 have most of their energy at higher frequencies than S3 and S4.

quiz.q: On a PCG, S1 begins 0.06 s after the R wave and S2 begins 0.38 s after the same R wave. The next R wave is 0.90 s later. Find the systolic interval, the diastolic interval and the heart rate.
quiz.a: Systolic interval = 0.38 − 0.06 = 0.32 s. Diastolic interval = 0.90 − 0.32 = 0.58 s. Heart rate = 60 / 0.90 = 66.7 beats per minute.

quiz.q: A PCG is recorded with a 25-400 Hz band-pass filter. A murmur has strong energy at 650 Hz. Explain what the trace will show.
quiz.a: The 650 Hz component is above the 400 Hz upper cutoff. The filter attenuates it heavily, so the murmur will be weak or absent on the trace even if it is present in the patient.
A2 and P2 are the aortic and pulmonary components of S2. They can separate slightly in time, often widening on inspiration, so S2 appears split.

quiz.q: Why is an ECG channel recorded together with the PCG?
quiz.a: The ECG gives a time reference. The R wave marks electrical activation, so S1, S2 and murmurs can be placed at fixed delays after it and timed against the cardiac cycle.

quiz.q: A stethoscope has tubing that is much longer and narrower than normal. Which heart sounds suffer most, and why?
quiz.a: High-frequency sounds suffer most. A long, narrow tube attenuates high frequencies more than low frequencies and can add resonances, so S1, S2 and high-frequency murmurs become weaker or distorted.

beyond: Not for the exam. Electronic stethoscopes now digitise the chest-piece signal, filter it in software and send it over Bluetooth for remote auscultation. Digital PCG is used in wearable patches and in foetal monitoring, where the baby's sound must be separated from the mother's. Research groups apply machine learning to PCG traces to classify murmurs, but the basic timing against ECG remains the reference. Search for electronic stethoscope, digital phonocardiography, cardiac auscultation and foetal phonocardiography.
